# Data

The data was downloaded from the StatsBomb Open Data repository by the script
`scripts/00_preuzmi_podatke.R`. For each of the four leagues (Premier League,
La Liga, Ligue 1, Serie A) the season with the largest number of matches is
chosen, and the download proceeds in an alternating (round-robin) fashion so
that the leagues are evenly represented. In total **1,517 matches** were
downloaded, i.e. **4.25 GB** of raw JSON files, one file per match. Match-level
metadata is kept in `all_matches_meta.csv`, while
`downloaded_matches_manifest.csv` (1,517 rows) contains only the matches that
were actually downloaded and is used as the reference when loading. After
parsing, the dataset contains **5,321,459 event records** and 18 features.

The data was used in accordance with the StatsBomb Open Data licence
(non-commercial, research use with mandatory attribution).

## Season selection and download

For each league the season with the largest number of played matches is chosen:

```{r code-season-selection}
base_url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/statsbomb/open-data/master/data"
target_leagues <- c("Premier League", "La Liga", "Ligue 1", "Serie A")

competitions <- fromJSON(file.path(base_url, "competitions.json"))
cand <- competitions[competitions$competition_name %in% target_leagues, ]

get_match_count <- function(comp_id, season_id) {
  url <- sprintf("%s/matches/%s/%s.json", base_url, comp_id, season_id)
  tryCatch(nrow(fromJSON(url)), error = function(e) NA_integer_)
}
cand$n_matches <- mapply(get_match_count, cand$competition_id, cand$season_id)

best_season <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(cand, cand$competition_name), function(df) {
  df[which.max(df$n_matches), ]
}))
```

The download alternates between leagues, counting bytes and skipping files that
have already been fetched, which makes the procedure interruptible and
resumable:

```{r code-download}
target_bytes <- 5 * 1024^3
downloaded_bytes <- 0
max_n <- max(sapply(match_lists, nrow))

for (row in seq_len(max_n)) {
  if (downloaded_bytes >= target_bytes) break
  for (league in names(match_lists)) {           # round-robin across leagues
    if (downloaded_bytes >= target_bytes) break
    m <- match_lists[[league]]
    if (row > nrow(m)) next                      # this league has run out of matches

    match_id <- m$match_id[row]
    dest <- file.path(events_dir, paste0(match_id, ".json"))
    if (file.exists(dest)) {                     # resuming an interrupted download
      downloaded_bytes <- downloaded_bytes + file.info(dest)$size
      next
    }
    ok <- tryCatch({
      download.file(sprintf("%s/events/%s.json", base_url, match_id),
                    dest, quiet = TRUE, mode = "wb"); TRUE
    }, error = function(e) FALSE)

    fsize <- if (ok && file.exists(dest)) file.info(dest)$size else 0
    if (fsize == 0) unlink(dest) else downloaded_bytes <- downloaded_bytes + fsize
    Sys.sleep(0.05)
  }
}
```

# Data processing in Spark

## Execution environment

The analysis was carried out in **Apache Spark 3.5.8** (Hadoop 3), installed
locally through the `sparklyr` package and started in `local[*]` mode, where a
single JVM process takes on the role of both driver and executor and uses all
available cores. The driver was given 8 GB of memory, the limit on the result
returned to the R session is 2 GB, and the number of partitions used in shuffle
operations was reduced from the default 200 to 32, which is more appropriate for
this data volume on a single machine.

```{r spark-conf}
PROJECT <- normalizePath(".", winslash = "/", mustWork = TRUE)
sp <- function(p) paste0("file:///", file.path(PROJECT, p, fsep = "/"))

conf <- spark_config()
conf$`sparklyr.shell.driver-memory` <- "8G"
conf$spark.driver.maxResultSize     <- "2G"
conf$spark.sql.shuffle.partitions   <- 32
sc <- spark_connect(master = "local[*]", version = "3.5", config = conf)
```

The helper function `sp()` exists because Spark runs on the JVM and expects a
URI rather than a Windows path; `normalizePath` yields an absolute path, and the
`file:///` prefix tells Spark to read from the local file system.

Packages used: `sparklyr` for working with Spark, `dplyr`, `tidyr` and `readr`
for processing, `ggplot2` and `dbplot` for visualisation, `caret` for the
confusion matrix and stratified folds, `kknn` for the k-nearest-neighbours
method, `pROC` for multiclass AUC, `cluster` for silhouette analysis and
`e1071` for the skewness coefficient.

## Loading and flattening the JSON structure

Processing takes place in two layers. First all JSON files are loaded and, by
flattening the nested structure, the Parquet dataset `data/interim/events_flat`
is formed, in which one row corresponds to one event. The match identifier is
extracted from the file name, since the records themselves do not contain it.

```{r code-json}
spark_read_json(sc, "raw", sp("data/raw/statsbomb/events"),
                options = list(multiLine = "true"), memory = FALSE)

DBI::dbExecute(sc, "
  CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP VIEW raw_id AS
  SELECT *,
         CAST(regexp_extract(input_file_name(), '([0-9]+)\\.json$', 1) AS INT) AS match_id
  FROM raw")

DBI::dbExecute(sc, "
  CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP VIEW ev AS
  SELECT match_id, minute, second,
         type.name              AS event_type,
         player.id              AS player_id,
         player.name            AS player_name,
         team.name              AS team_name,
         position.name          AS position_name,
         pass.outcome.name      AS pass_outcome,
         pass.length            AS pass_length,
         pass.goal_assist       AS pass_goal_assist,
         pass.shot_assist       AS pass_shot_assist,
         shot.statsbomb_xg      AS shot_xg,
         shot.outcome.name      AS shot_outcome,
         dribble.outcome.name   AS dribble_outcome,
         duel.type.name         AS duel_type,
         location[0]            AS loc_x,
         location[1]            AS loc_y
  FROM raw_id")

spark_write_parquet(tbl(sc, "ev"), sp("data/interim/events_flat"), mode = "overwrite")
```

## Computing minutes played

Minutes played are reconstructed from three types of administrative event. The
end of a match is the maximum time among the *Half End* records, which also
covers stoppage time. Starters play until they are substituted off or until the
end, substitutes from the moment they come on until the end. Only players with
at least **450 minutes played** are included in the analysis.

```{r code-minutes}
DBI::dbExecute(sc, "
  CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP VIEW match_end AS
  SELECT match_id, MAX(minute + second/60.0) AS end_min
  FROM raw_id WHERE type.name = 'Half End' GROUP BY match_id")

DBI::dbExecute(sc, "
  CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP VIEW starters AS
  SELECT r.match_id, p.player.id AS player_id, r.team.name AS team_name
  FROM raw_id r
  LATERAL VIEW explode(r.tactics.lineup) lu AS p
  WHERE r.type.name = 'Starting XI'")

DBI::dbExecute(sc, "
  CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP VIEW subs AS
  SELECT match_id, player.id AS off_id,
         substitution.replacement.id AS on_id,
         team.name AS team_name, minute + second/60.0 AS sub_min
  FROM raw_id WHERE type.name = 'Substitution'")

DBI::dbExecute(sc, "
  CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP VIEW minutes_match AS
  SELECT s.match_id, s.player_id, s.team_name,
         COALESCE(sb.sub_min, m.end_min) AS mins     -- starter: until substituted off or until the end
  FROM starters s
  JOIN match_end m ON m.match_id = s.match_id
  LEFT JOIN subs sb ON sb.match_id = s.match_id AND sb.off_id = s.player_id
  UNION ALL
  SELECT sb.match_id, sb.on_id, sb.team_name,
         m.end_min - sb.sub_min AS mins              -- substitute: from coming on until the end
  FROM subs sb JOIN match_end m ON m.match_id = sb.match_id")
```

## Aggregation into counters and normalisation

All counters are formed in a **single pass** over the event layer, by
conditional summation per event type. The key is the player–team combination, so
a player who changed clubs produces two separate rows.

```{r code-counters}
DBI::dbExecute(sc, "
  CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP VIEW counts AS
  SELECT player_id, team_name, MAX(player_name) AS player,
    SUM(CASE WHEN event_type='Pass' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS passes,
    SUM(CASE WHEN event_type='Pass' AND pass_outcome IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS passes_completed,
    SUM(CASE WHEN event_type='Pass' AND pass_length >= 30 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS long_passes,
    SUM(CASE WHEN pass_shot_assist = true THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS key_passes,
    SUM(CASE WHEN pass_goal_assist = true THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS assists,
    SUM(CASE WHEN event_type='Shot' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS shots,
    SUM(COALESCE(shot_xg, 0)) AS xg,
    SUM(CASE WHEN event_type='Clearance' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS clearances,
    SUM(CASE WHEN event_type='Duel' AND duel_type='Tackle' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS tackles,
    -- ... the remaining counters have the same form ...
    AVG(loc_x) AS mean_x, AVG(loc_y) AS mean_y,
    STDDEV(loc_x) AS sd_x, STDDEV(loc_y) AS sd_y,
    SUM(CASE WHEN loc_x >= 80 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS touches_f3,
    SUM(CASE WHEN loc_x <= 40 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS touches_d3,
    COUNT(*) AS n_events
  FROM ev_p WHERE player_id IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY player_id, team_name")
```

The counters are then normalised to 90 minutes, and the query is generated
programmatically so that 22 expressions do not have to be written by hand:

```{r code-p90}
cnt_fields <- c("passes","passes_completed","long_passes","key_passes","assists",
                "carries","shots","goals","xg","dribbles","dribbles_completed",
                "pressures","ball_recoveries","interceptions","clearances",
                "blocks","duels","tackles","fouls","dispossessed","miscontrols",
                "ball_receipts")

p90_sql <- paste(sprintf("ROUND(c.%s / m.minutes * 90, 3) AS %s_p90",
                         cnt_fields, cnt_fields), collapse = ",\n  ")

final_sql <- sprintf("
  SELECT c.player_id, c.player, c.team_name AS team,
         p.position, p.pos_purity, ROUND(m.minutes, 1) AS minutes,
         %s,
         ROUND(c.passes_completed / GREATEST(c.passes, 1), 3)   AS pass_completion_pct,
         ROUND(c.pass_length_sum  / GREATEST(c.passes, 1), 2)   AS avg_pass_length,
         ROUND(c.mean_x, 2) AS mean_x, ROUND(c.mean_y, 2) AS mean_y,
         ROUND(c.sd_x, 2)   AS sd_x,   ROUND(c.sd_y, 2)   AS sd_y,
         ROUND(c.touches_f3 / c.n_events, 3) AS f3_share,
         ROUND(c.touches_d3 / c.n_events, 3) AS d3_share
  FROM counts c
  JOIN minutes_total m ON m.player_id = c.player_id AND m.team_name = c.team_name
  LEFT JOIN positions p ON p.player_id = c.player_id AND p.team_name = c.team_name
  WHERE m.minutes >= %d", p90_sql, 450)

feat <- sdf_sql(sc, final_sql)
spark_write_parquet(sdf_repartition(feat, 1), sp("data/interim/player_features"),
                    mode = "overwrite")
```

# Target feature and label quality

The target feature was formed by mapping the detailed StatsBomb positions into
six positional classes: **GK, CB, FB, DM_CM, AM_W, FW** (22 of the 24 possible
positions appear in the dataset).

```{r code-positions}
position_group <- case_when(
  position == "Goalkeeper" ~ "GK",
  position %in% c("Right Center Back", "Left Center Back", "Center Back") ~ "CB",
  position %in% c("Left Back", "Right Back",
                  "Left Wing Back", "Right Wing Back") ~ "FB",
  position %in% c("Right Defensive Midfield", "Left Defensive Midfield",
                  "Center Defensive Midfield", "Right Center Midfield",
                  "Left Center Midfield") ~ "DM_CM",
  position %in% c("Right Wing", "Left Wing", "Center Attacking Midfield",
                  "Right Attacking Midfield", "Right Midfield",
                  "Left Midfield") ~ "AM_W",
  position %in% c("Center Forward", "Right Center Forward",
                  "Left Center Forward") ~ "FW"
)
```

A player's position was determined as the **modal** one, while at the same time
computing its **purity** — the share of events played in that position. A window
function computes the total number of events as the denominator, and the ranking
picks the most frequent position:

```{r code-purity}
DBI::dbExecute(sc, "
  CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP VIEW pos_rank AS
  SELECT player_id, team_name, position_name, cnt, total,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY player_id, team_name ORDER BY cnt DESC) AS rk
  FROM (
    SELECT player_id, team_name, position_name,
           COUNT(*) AS cnt,
           SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER (PARTITION BY player_id, team_name) AS total
    FROM ev_p
    WHERE player_id IS NOT NULL AND position_name IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY player_id, team_name, position_name)")

DBI::dbExecute(sc, "
  CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP VIEW positions AS
  SELECT player_id, team_name, position_name AS position,
         ROUND(cnt / total, 3) AS pos_purity
  FROM pos_rank WHERE rk = 1")
```

The first computation, over the detailed positions, gave a median of 0.676, with
456 rows (27%) below 0.5. On closer inspection it was established that this is
an artefact of the granularity of the feature rather than genuine ambiguity of
the role: rotation between the left and the right centre-back counts as impurity
even though the positional class stays the same. The measure was therefore
recomputed over the six classes.

| Aggregation level | Min | Q1 | Median | Mean | Q3 | Max | Share below 0.5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 22 detailed positions | 0.194 | 0.487 | 0.676 | 0.687 | 0.923 | 1.000 | 456 (26.8%) |
| 6 positional classes | 0.389 | 0.855 | 0.979 | 0.904 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 25 (1.5%) |

At the level of six classes the median purity is 0.979, and three quarters of
the players have a purity above 0.855, which confirms that the target feature is
not noisy. The remaining 25 rows represent genuinely multi-positional players;
they were not removed but kept and used when interpreting classification errors.

```{r figure1, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Figure 1: Conceptual division of the pitch by positional class"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/podela_pozicija.png")
```

# Missing value analysis

The analysis was carried out over the event dataset (5,321,459 records, 18
features) rather than over the derived player-level table, because aggregation
into counters makes missing values disappear. The per-column profile is obtained
with a single query, generated programmatically over the column names:

```{r code-na-profile}
cols <- colnames(ev)
na_sql <- paste(sprintf("SUM(CASE WHEN %s IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS %s", cols, cols),
                collapse = ", ")
na_prof <- sdf_sql(sc, sprintf("SELECT COUNT(*) AS n_total, %s FROM ev_p", na_sql)) %>%
  collect()

na_tbl <- data.frame(
  column = cols,
  n_na   = as.numeric(na_prof[1, cols]),
  pct_na = round(100 * as.numeric(na_prof[1, cols]) / na_prof$n_total, 1)
)
na_tbl[order(-na_tbl$pct_na), ]
```

Five features have no missing values at all, while seven have a share above 70%.
None of the missing values is the consequence of a collection error — they all
fall into four categories:

- **Structural absence** — `shot_xg`, `shot_outcome`, `dribble_outcome`,
  `duel_type` and `pass_length` are defined only for the corresponding event
  type. A check shows a perfect match: `shot_xg` is missing in 5,283,571
  records, exactly as many as there are non-shot events, while among the 37,888
  shots it is not missing in a single one.
- **Semantic absence** — for `pass_outcome` a value is written only when the
  pass failed, so NA denotes success. Of 1,481,813 passes, 1,136,687 have no
  outcome recorded, which gives an accuracy of 76.7%. This is the only case in
  which naively dropping such records would give an accuracy of 0% for every
  player.
- **Logical absence** — the boolean features `pass_goal_assist` and
  `pass_shot_assist` are written only when the condition is satisfied (2,596
  assists and 24,439 key passes).
- **Administrative events** — *Half Start*, *Starting XI*, *Tactical Shift*:
  20,393 (0.4%) records without a player and 37,460 (0.7%) without coordinates.

The structural-absence hypothesis was checked by comparing across event types:

```{r code-na-check}
# confirmation that shot_xg is missing exactly where the event is not a shot
sdf_sql(sc, "
  SELECT event_type, COUNT(*) AS n,
         ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN shot_xg IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)/COUNT(*), 1) AS pct_na_xg,
         ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN loc_x   IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)/COUNT(*), 1) AS pct_na_loc,
         ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN player_id IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)/COUNT(*), 1) AS pct_na_player
  FROM ev_p GROUP BY event_type ORDER BY n DESC") %>% collect()

# confirmation that NA in pass_outcome means a completed pass
ev %>% filter(!is.na(pass_outcome)) %>% count(pass_outcome, sort = TRUE) %>% collect()
```

No imputation method was applied. The counters were formed by conditional
summation per event type (structural absence yields a zero), `pass_outcome IS
NULL` was used as the definition of a completed pass, records without a player
were excluded by a condition on the identifier, and `AVG` and `STDDEV` ignore
missing coordinates. **The final player-level table contains no missing values
at all.**

# Preliminary analysis

The analysis was carried out at two levels: over the event dataset (5,321,459
records) in Spark and over the derived player-level table (1,702 rows) in R.
The split follows the principle behind the `sparklyr` package — the processing
is executed in Spark, and only aggregated results are collected into R.

## Event level

33 event types were recorded, with passes, ball receipts and carries accounting
for 74.8% of all records.

| event_type | n |
|---|---|
| Pass | 1,481,813 |
| Ball Receipt* | 1,384,869 |
| Carry | 1,117,196 |
| Pressure | 491,104 |
| Ball Recovery | 162,682 |
| Duel | 125,123 |
| Clearance | 73,006 |
| Block | 59,169 |

*Table 1: The most frequent event types*

The **dbplot** package was used to visualise the distributions; it computes the
binned distribution in Spark and transfers into R only the table of per-bin
values, thereby avoiding the transfer of 1.48 million individual values.

```{r code-dbplot}
ev %>% filter(!is.na(pass_length)) %>%
  dbplot_histogram(pass_length, bins = 60) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of pass length",
       subtitle = "1,481,813 passes, aggregation performed in Spark",
       x = "Pass length (yards)", y = "Number of passes")
ggsave("figures/A2_pass_length.png", width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 150)

ev %>% filter(!is.na(loc_x), !is.na(loc_y)) %>%
  dbplot_raster(loc_x, loc_y, resolution = 60) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  labs(title = "Touch density across the pitch", subtitle = "5.28 million records",
       x = "Pitch length", y = "Pitch width")
ggsave("figures/A3_heatmap.png", width = 9, height = 6, dpi = 150)
```

```{r a2, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Figure 2: Histogram of pass length"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/A2_pass_length.png")
```

The distribution of pass length is markedly right-skewed, with a peak in the
range of short passes and a tail corresponding to long balls and crosses.

```{r a3, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Figure 3: Touch density across the pitch"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/A3_heatmap.png")
```

For the display by positional class the coordinates were reduced to a grid with
a step of four units, by integer division **inside the query**, which reduces
the set of 5.28 million records to a few thousand aggregated cells before the
transfer into R:

```{r code-heatmap-positions}
grid <- sdf_sql(sc, "
  SELECT CASE
    WHEN position_name='Goalkeeper' THEN 'GK'
    WHEN position_name IN ('Right Center Back','Left Center Back','Center Back') THEN 'CB'
    WHEN position_name IN ('Left Back','Right Back','Left Wing Back','Right Wing Back') THEN 'FB'
    WHEN position_name IN ('Right Defensive Midfield','Left Defensive Midfield',
         'Center Defensive Midfield','Right Center Midfield','Left Center Midfield') THEN 'DM_CM'
    WHEN position_name IN ('Right Wing','Left Wing','Center Attacking Midfield',
         'Right Attacking Midfield','Right Midfield','Left Midfield') THEN 'AM_W'
    WHEN position_name IN ('Center Forward','Right Center Forward','Left Center Forward') THEN 'FW'
  END AS pos_grp,
  FLOOR(loc_x/4)*4 AS gx, FLOOR(loc_y/4)*4 AS gy, COUNT(*) AS n
  FROM ev_p WHERE loc_x IS NOT NULL AND position_name IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY 1,2,3") %>% collect()

grid$pos_grp <- factor(grid$pos_grp, levels = c("GK","CB","FB","DM_CM","AM_W","FW"))
ggplot(grid, aes(gx, gy, fill = n)) + geom_tile() +
  facet_wrap(~ pos_grp) + scale_fill_viridis_c(trans = "sqrt") +
  labs(title = "Touch density by positional class", x = NULL, y = NULL)
ggsave("figures/A4_heatmap_pozicije.png", width = 11, height = 7, dpi = 150)
```

```{r a4, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Figure 4: Touch density by positional class"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/A4_heatmap_pozicije.png")
```

The display by class shows clearly delineated patterns: goalkeepers are
exclusively inside their own penalty area, centre-backs in front of it,
full-backs along the touchlines, midfielders have the most even distribution
around the central axis, wingers repeat the full-backs' pattern but shifted
towards the opposition half, and forwards are concentrated in the opposition
penalty area. The differences are visible to the naked eye and constitute the
first confirmation that the positional classes are separable from the data. The
display also foreshadows where errors are to be expected: full-backs and wingers
differ mainly in their position along the length of the pitch rather than in the
shape of the pattern, while centre-backs and defensive midfielders overlap in
front of their own penalty area.

## Descriptive statistics and distributions

For each of the 31 numeric features the mean, median, standard deviation,
minimum, maximum and skewness coefficient were computed.

```{r code-descriptives}
d <- read.csv("data/processed/player_features_labeled.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
d$position_group <- factor(d$position_group, levels = c("GK","CB","FB","DM_CM","AM_W","FW"))

num <- names(d)[sapply(d, is.numeric)]
num <- setdiff(num, c("player_id", "pos_purity", "purity6", "minutes"))

desc <- data.frame(
  obelezje   = num,
  sredina    = sapply(d[num], mean),
  medijana   = sapply(d[num], median),
  sd         = sapply(d[num], sd),
  min        = sapply(d[num], min),
  max        = sapply(d[num], max),
  asimetrija = sapply(d[num], e1071::skewness)
)
desc[, -1] <- round(desc[, -1], 3)
write.csv(desc, "results/deskriptiva.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r descriptives-table, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE}
if (!is.null(descriptives)) {
  descriptives |> arrange(desc(abs(asimetrija))) |> head(12) |>
    tab("Table 2 — The twelve features with the most pronounced skewness", digits = 3)
}
```

> Column names in the table: `obelezje` = feature, `sredina` = mean,
> `medijana` = median, `asimetrija` = skewness.

The correctness of the table was checked by comparing the extreme values against
individual cases: the lowest pass completion is 0.391 and belongs to a
goalkeeper, which matches the value from the preparation stage. The widest range
belongs to `mean_x`, from 7.18 to 86.47, thereby covering practically the entire
length of the pitch.

```{r code-distributions}
d %>% select(all_of(num)) %>% pivot_longer(everything()) %>%
  ggplot(aes(value)) + geom_histogram(bins = 40) +
  facet_wrap(~ name, scales = "free", ncol = 5) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of the player-level features")
ggsave("figures/B2_raspodele.png", width = 15, height = 12, dpi = 130)
```

```{r b2, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Figure 5: Histograms of all player-level features"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/B2_raspodele.png")
```

Positive skewness is most pronounced for `goals_p90` (2.29), `xg_p90` (1.96) and
`assists_p90` (1.87); for goals the mean is 0.113 and the median 0.054, which
reflects the genuine nature of the phenomenon. The negative skewness of `sd_x`
(−1.58) and `mean_x` (−1.08) is a consequence of the presence of goalkeepers.

No feature transformation was carried out: the decision tree and the random
forest are insensitive to monotone transformations, while for the k-nearest
neighbours method the influence of the tails is mitigated by standardisation
inside the pipeline, within every cross-validation fold.

## Relationships between features

```{r code-correlations}
cm <- cor(d[num])
ggcorrplot::ggcorrplot(cm, hc.order = TRUE, type = "lower", tl.cex = 7) +
  labs(title = "Correlations between features")
ggsave("figures/B3_pirsonov_koeficijent_korelacije.png", width = 11, height = 10, dpi = 150)

# pairs with an absolute correlation above 0.8
cp <- as.data.frame(as.table(cm))
cp <- cp[cp$Var1 != cp$Var2 & abs(cp$Freq) > 0.8, ]
cp <- cp[!duplicated(t(apply(cp[, 1:2], 1, sort))), ]
cp[order(-abs(cp$Freq)), ]
```

Pearson correlation coefficients were computed for all 465 feature pairs, of
which 16 have an absolute value above 0.8. The strongest relationships are
`d3_share`–`mean_x` (−0.980), `passes_completed_p90`–`passes_p90` (0.975) and
`dribbles_completed_p90`–`dribbles_p90` (0.956).

```{r b3, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Figure 6: Pearson correlation coefficients"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/B3_pirsonov_koeficijent_korelacije.png")
```

The features `passes_completed_p90` and `dribbles_completed_p90` were removed
from the modelling set; they are the product of the corresponding counter and
the success percentage, so in distance-based methods they cause the same
quantity to be counted more than once. **The final set contains 29 features.**
The pair `d3_share`–`mean_x` was kept in full, since neither is derived from the
other and both are near the top in discriminative power; their redundancy is
covered by the scenario with dimensionality reduction.

To assess discriminative power, a one-way analysis of variance was applied with
the positional class as the factor:

```{r code-anova}
fvals <- sapply(num, function(v) summary(aov(d[[v]] ~ d$position_group))[[1]][1, 4])
head(sort(fvals, decreasing = TRUE), 12)

top8 <- names(head(sort(fvals, decreasing = TRUE), 8))
d %>% select(position_group, all_of(top8)) %>%
  pivot_longer(-position_group) %>%
  ggplot(aes(position_group, value, fill = position_group)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.4) + facet_wrap(~ name, scales = "free_y") +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(title = "The features that best separate the positional classes", x = NULL)
ggsave("figures/B5_boxplot.png", width = 12, height = 8, dpi = 150)
```

| Feature | F | Feature | F |
|---|---|---|---|
| `d3_share` | 8,586.5 | `clearances_p90` | 1,523.1 |
| `mean_x` | 6,953.7 | `miscontrols_p90` | 1,069.5 |
| `avg_pass_length` | 3,036.9 | `pressures_p90` | 719.6 |
| `sd_x` | 2,601.0 | `shots_p90` | 695.4 |
| `f3_share` | 2,451.9 | `long_passes_p90` | 691.0 |

*Table 3: The features that best separate the positions (ANOVA F)*

Four of the five most discriminative features are spatial in nature. The
strongest spatial feature, `d3_share`, has 5.6 times the discriminative power of
the strongest event counter, `clearances_p90`. A player's position is therefore
read more reliably from **where** the player moves than from **which** actions
they perform. The spatial features were not part of the initial version of the
table and were introduced only when the processing was moved to Spark.

```{r b5, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Figure 7: Box plots of the most discriminative features by class"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/B5_boxplot.png")
```

## Principal component analysis

```{r code-pca}
pca <- prcomp(d[num], scale. = TRUE)
ve <- round(100 * summary(pca)$importance[2, 1:5], 1); ve
which(cumsum(summary(pca)$importance[2, ]) >= 0.9)[1]   # number of components for 90%

ggplot(data.frame(PC1 = pca$x[, 1], PC2 = pca$x[, 2], poz = d$position_group),
       aes(PC1, PC2, color = poz)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 1.6) +
  labs(title = sprintf("PCA — PC1 %.1f%%, PC2 %.1f%%", ve[1], ve[2]))
ggsave("figures/B6_pca.png", width = 8, height = 6, dpi = 150)
```

Over the standardised dataset the first principal component explains 37.6% of
the variance, the second 18.7% and the third 10.3%. Capturing 90% of the
variance requires 11 components, which numerically confirms the redundancy
observed earlier; that value was adopted as the parameter for the scenario with
dimensionality reduction. The first two components carry 56.3%, enough for a
two-dimensional display that is later used to show the clusters as well.

```{r b6, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Figure 8: Principal component analysis"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/B6_pca.png")
```

Goalkeepers stand out as a completely separate group, without a single overlap.
The remaining five classes form a **continuum** along the first component,
ordered from centre-backs through full-backs and midfielders to wingers and
forwards, with no sharp boundaries between neighbouring classes. The finding
indicates that positional roles are not discrete categories but points on a
spectrum, so classification errors are expected to be concentrated between
neighbouring classes.

# Preparing the modelling dataset

The preparation is performed once, and its results are used unchanged by all
three classification methods, which makes the results comparable.

```{r code-featcols}
num <- setdiff(names(d)[sapply(d, is.numeric)],
               c("player_id", "pos_purity", "purity6", "minutes"))
feat_cols <- setdiff(num, c("passes_completed_p90", "dribbles_completed_p90"))
saveRDS(feat_cols, "results/feat_cols.rds")   # 29 features
```

The data was transferred into Spark with the `copy_to` function and split in an
80 : 20 ratio. The test set is not used during model and parameter selection;
its only purpose is to evaluate the finally chosen solutions.

The `sdf_random_split` function does not guarantee stratification by class. With
an imbalanced dataset in which the smallest class has 125 rows, a random split
may deviate substantially from the desired ratio and make the per-class
estimates unstable. The split was therefore carried out with a window function:
every row was assigned a random value with a fixed seed, within each class the
percentile rank was computed with the `percent_rank` function, and the cut-off
was set at 0.8.

```{r code-split}
tbl <- copy_to(sc, d[, c("player", "team", "position_group", feat_cols)],
               "players", overwrite = TRUE)

strat <- tbl %>%
  group_by(position_group) %>%
  mutate(rk = percent_rank(rand(42L))) %>%
  ungroup()

train <- strat %>% filter(rk <= 0.8) %>% select(-rk) %>% compute("train")
test  <- strat %>% filter(rk >  0.8) %>% select(-rk) %>% compute("test")

spark_write_parquet(train, sp("data/interim/train"), mode = "overwrite")
spark_write_parquet(test,  sp("data/interim/test"),  mode = "overwrite")
```

| Class | Total | Train | Test | Share in training |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GK | 125 | 100 | 25 | 80.0% |
| CB | 300 | 240 | 60 | 80.0% |
| FB | 332 | 265 | 67 | 79.8% |
| DM_CM | 368 | 294 | 74 | 79.9% |
| AM_W | 360 | 288 | 72 | 80.0% |
| FW | 217 | 173 | 44 | 79.7% |
| **Total** | **1,702** | **1,360** | **342** | **79.9%** |

*Table 4: The achieved split by positional class*

The share of the training part is between 79.7% and 80.0% in every class,
including the smallest one, so stratification was fully achieved. Both tables
were saved in Parquet format, so the k-nearest-neighbours method, which runs in
R, uses an identical split. The random seed was fixed at 42 for full
reproducibility.

# Classification

## Common setup

Three classification models were built for the same target feature: a
**decision tree**, a **random forest** and the **k-nearest-neighbours method**.
All three use the same 29 features and an identical split, so differences in the
results stem exclusively from the methods themselves.

The tree and the forest were implemented through an `ml_pipeline` with four
stages:

```{r code-pipeline}
base_pipeline <- ml_pipeline(sc) %>%
  ft_string_indexer("position_group", "label") %>%                    # text -> numeric label
  ft_vector_assembler(input_cols = feat_cols, output_col = "features_raw") %>%
  ft_standard_scaler("features_raw", "features",
                     with_mean = TRUE, with_std = TRUE)

evaluator <- ml_multiclass_classification_evaluator(
  sc, label_col = "label", prediction_col = "prediction", metric_name = "f1")

run_cv <- function(grid, pipe) {
  cv <- ml_cross_validator(sc, estimator = pipe, estimator_param_maps = grid,
                           evaluator = evaluator, num_folds = 10,
                           parallelism = 4, seed = 42)
  ml_fit(cv, train)
}
```

Placing the standardisation **inside** the pipeline has a methodological
consequence. Since the whole pipeline is passed to the cross-validation object
as a single unit, the standardisation parameters are refitted in each of the ten
folds, and exclusively over the training data of that fold. This rules out the
information leakage that would occur if standardisation had been carried out
over the entire training set before the split into folds.

Standardisation is not necessary for the tree and the forest, since branching
decisions are made by comparison against thresholds. It was kept so that all
three methods use identical preparation.

The **weighted F1 measure** was used as the performance measure, chosen instead
of plain accuracy because of class imbalance, where the ratio of the most
numerous to the least numerous class is 2.9 : 1. Cross-validation was carried
out with ten folds, with `parallelism = 4` — the folds are mutually independent,
so the job is almost ideally parallel.

The Spark MLlib library **has no k-nearest-neighbours classifier** — it only
offers an LSH-based approximation of the neighbourhood, without a classification
head. That method was therefore implemented in R, with the `kknn` package.

## Decision tree

```{r code-dt-grids}
pipe_dt <- base_pipeline %>%
  ml_decision_tree_classifier(features_col = "features", label_col = "label")

g1 <- list(decision_tree = list(max_depth = c(2, 3, 5, 8, 12, 20)))
g2 <- list(decision_tree = list(min_instances_per_node = c(1, 5, 10, 20, 50),
                                min_info_gain = c(0, 0.001, 0.01)))
g3 <- list(decision_tree = list(impurity = c("gini", "entropy"),
                                max_depth = c(5, 10, 15)))

t1 <- system.time(cv1 <- run_cv(g1, pipe_dt))
t2 <- system.time(cv2 <- run_cv(g2, pipe_dt))
t3 <- system.time(cv3 <- run_cv(g3, pipe_dt))

vm1 <- ml_validation_metrics(cv1) %>% arrange(desc(f1))
vm2 <- ml_validation_metrics(cv2) %>% arrange(desc(f1))
vm3 <- ml_validation_metrics(cv3) %>% arrange(desc(f1))
```

The column names returned by `ml_validation_metrics` carry the suffix of the
pipeline stage (`max_depth_1`), so they cannot be hard-coded in the plotting
code. A helper function finds the name by pattern:

```{r code-pick}
pick <- function(vm, pat) names(vm)[grepl(pat, names(vm), ignore.case = TRUE)][1]

ggplot(vm1, aes(.data[[pick(vm1, "max_depth")]], f1)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  labs(title = "Decision tree, scenario 1: tree depth",
       subtitle = "F1 measure, 10-fold cross-validation",
       x = "Maximum depth", y = "F1")
ggsave("figures/DT_S1.png", width = 7, height = 4.5, dpi = 150)
```

### Scenario 1 — tree depth

```{r dt-s1, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE}
tab(dt_s1, "Table 5 — Decision tree, scenario 1: maximum depth")
```

```{r dt-s1-fig, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Figure 9: Decision tree, effect of the maximum depth"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/DT_S1.png")
```

The curve shows a clearly pronounced bias–variance trade-off. At depth 2 the
tree has at most four leaves, which is not enough to distinguish six classes, so
the F1 measure drops to 0.5299. Moving to depth 3 makes performance rise
sharply; it reaches its maximum at depth 5 and afterwards declines slightly but
steadily, which indicates overfitting. In the range from depth 3 to 20 the
difference between the best and the lowest value is only 2.3 percentage points,
from which it follows that the choice of depth, provided it is not trivially
small, is not decisive.

### Scenario 2 — branching stopping conditions

```{r dt-s2, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE}
tab(dt_s2, "Table 6 — Decision tree, scenario 2: stopping conditions")
```

```{r dt-s2-fig, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Figure 10: Decision tree, branching stopping conditions"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/DT_S2.png")
```

The `min_info_gain` parameter has practically no effect on the result: the
values 0 and 0.001 give identical results in all cases, while 0.01 makes a
difference only at the smallest values of the other parameter. The splits the
tree chooses are already informative enough, so the information-gain threshold
rarely becomes an active constraint. In the figure the curve for the value 0 is
not visible because it is completely covered by the other two — this is not a
shortcoming of the display but a consequence of the results being identical.

Increasing the minimum number of instances in a node reduces the F1 measure
overall, from 0.8852 at the value 1 to 0.8707 at the value 50, although the
decline is not strictly monotone. The total range across all 15 combinations is
1.5 percentage points.

### Scenario 3 — branching criterion

```{r dt-s3, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE}
tab(dt_s3, "Table 7 — Decision tree, scenario 3: impurity criterion")
```

```{r dt-s3-fig, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Figure 11: Decision tree, Gini index versus entropy"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/DT_S3.png")
```

Entropy gives a better result at every depth examined, and its advantage grows
with depth: 0.13 percentage points at depth 5, then 0.86 at depth 10 and 1.78 at
depth 15. The explanation is that entropy penalises node impurity more strongly
than the Gini index, so at greater depths, when nodes cover a smaller number of
examples, it makes more cautious branching decisions and overfits more slowly.
At smaller depths the difference is negligible, which is consistent with the
generally accepted finding that the choice of impurity criterion rarely has a
material effect on the performance of a tree.

### Choice of solution and evaluation on the test set

The best scenario is chosen by the highest mean F1 measure from
cross-validation, and `best_model` has already been refitted over the entire
training set:

```{r code-dt-choice}
best_f1   <- c(S1 = max(vm1$f1), S2 = max(vm2$f1), S3 = max(vm3$f1))
best_scen <- names(which.max(best_f1))
best_cv   <- list(S1 = cv1, S2 = cv2, S3 = cv3)[[best_scen]]
best_model <- best_cv$best_model
```

The model predicts numeric labels, so before the confusion matrix the
index → class-name dictionary must be reconstructed:

```{r code-dt-test}
map_lab <- ml_transform(best_model, train) %>%
  select(position_group, label) %>% distinct() %>% collect()

preds <- ml_transform(best_model, test) %>%
  select(position_group, label, prediction) %>% collect() %>%
  left_join(map_lab, by = c("prediction" = "label"), suffix = c("", "_pred")) %>%
  rename(pred_group = position_group_pred)

lvl <- c("GK","CB","FB","DM_CM","AM_W","FW")   # order from defence to attack
cm <- caret::confusionMatrix(factor(preds$pred_group,     levels = lvl),
                             factor(preds$position_group, levels = lvl))
```

The order of the levels is not alphabetical but runs from defence to attack, so
that the structure of the errors in the matrix is visible.

Comparing the best results per scenario — 0.8844 for the first, 0.8852 for the
second and 0.8857 for the third — the model from the third scenario was chosen,
with the entropy criterion and a maximum depth of 5. The best results of all
three scenarios differ by less than 0.15 percentage points, from which it
follows that the method has reached its ceiling on the available data.

| Indicator | Value |
|---|---|
| F1 from cross-validation (10 folds) | 0.8857 |
| Accuracy on the test set | 0.9123 |
| 95% confidence interval | (0.877 – 0.940) |
| Cohen's kappa | 0.8926 |
| Macro precision | 0.9276 |
| Macro recall | 0.9191 |
| Macro F1 | 0.9226 |
| Balanced accuracy | 0.9504 |
| Multiclass AUC (Hand–Till) | 0.9776 |
| Training time for a single model | 2.6 s |
| Prediction time over the test set | 0.5 s |
| Number of models trained in the search | 273 |

*Table 8: Performance indicators of the selected decision tree*

An accuracy of 91.2% substantially exceeds the majority-class rate of 21.6%,
with p < 0.001. Cohen's kappa of 0.8926 shows almost perfect agreement with the
true labels.

The multiclass AUC is the only indicator that is not derived from the confusion
matrix. The remaining measures evaluate the model's final decision, while the
AUC is computed from the distribution of per-class probabilities and measures
how reliably the model separates the classes before making a decision. The
probabilities are obtained by decomposing the vector column `probability`:

```{r code-auc}
probs <- ml_transform(best_model, test) %>%
  sdf_separate_column("probability", into = paste0("p", 0:5)) %>%
  select(label, p0, p1, p2, p3, p4, p5) %>% collect()

pmat <- as.matrix(probs[, paste0("p", 0:5)])
colnames(pmat) <- as.character(0:5)

auc <- pROC::multiclass.roc(response = factor(probs$label, levels = 0:5),
                            predictor = pmat)
```

The macro F1 on the test set (0.9226) is higher than the value from
cross-validation (0.8857). The difference has two sources: cross-validation
trains each model over nine tenths of the training set, so it gives a slightly
pessimistic estimate, and the measures applied are not identical — Spark
computes an F1 weighted by the number of examples per class, whereas macro F1 is
a plain arithmetic mean over the classes, which the goalkeeper class, with its
perfect result, pushes upwards.

```{r dt-by-class, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE}
tab(dt_by_class, "Table 9 — Decision tree: performance by positional class")
```

The goalkeeper class was classified perfectly on every indicator. That result is
not a genuine achievement of the model: goalkeepers have feature values that do
not overlap with any other class, which is also visible in the principal
component plot. The class is therefore treated as trivial in the interpretation,
with the note that it raises the values of the macro measures.

The hardest class is that of attacking midfielders and wingers, with an F1
measure of 0.8630. That class makes errors in both directions towards both
neighbouring classes. The class of defensive and central midfielders has the
lowest precision alongside a high recall, from which it follows that the model
has a tendency to place borderline cases into it.

```{r dt-confusion, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Figure 12: Confusion matrix — decision tree"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/DT_confusion.png")
```

Of 342 examples, 312 were classified correctly and 30 incorrectly. All the
populated cells lie on the diagonal or in its immediate vicinity, while the
corners of the matrix are empty. **Twenty-nine of the 30 errors occur between
classes that are neighbours on the defence–attack spectrum.** The only exception
is a full-back placed among the wingers; even that case is not arbitrary, since
full-backs and wingers share a movement pattern along the touchlines.

The project specification assumed that the most frequent errors would be between
related positions, with full-backs and centre-backs given as an example. The
hypothesis was confirmed in its general form, but the stated example was not:
the centre-back–full-back pair has just one error and is among the best
separated. The dominant confusions occur in the attacking part of the spectrum.

The structure of the selected tree and the feature importances are read directly
from the Scala object through the JVM bridge, since sparklyr does not expose all
MLlib methods:

```{r code-dt-structure}
dt_stage <- ml_stage(best_model, 4)          # the 4th pipeline stage is the classifier
imp <- spark_jobj(dt_stage) %>% invoke("featureImportances") %>% invoke("toArray")

imp_df <- data.frame(obelezje = feat_cols, znacaj = round(imp, 4)) %>%
  arrange(desc(znacaj))

cat("Depth:", invoke(spark_jobj(dt_stage), "depth"),
    "| Number of nodes:", invoke(spark_jobj(dt_stage), "numNodes"), "\n")

writeLines(invoke(spark_jobj(dt_stage), "toDebugString"),
           "results/dt_tree_structure.txt")   # the whole tree as a set of rules
```

```{r dt-importance, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Figure 13: Feature importance — decision tree"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/DT_importance.png")
```

The selected tree has a depth of 5 and 33 nodes in total, of which 16 are
internal splits and 17 are leaves. The first four features carry 89.6% of the
total importance, with `mean_x` alone carrying 60.3% — more than all the
remaining 28 features together.

A comparison with the analysis of variance reveals two phenomena. First,
**correlated features suppress one another**: `d3_share` was the most
discriminative feature on its own, but it correlates −0.980 with `mean_x`, which
the tree chooses for its first split and thereby exhausts that information.
Second, **the tree rewards complementary information**: `interceptions_p90` was
not among the top twelve by the analysis of variance, but it is third by
importance in the tree, because it distinguishes a defensive midfielder from a
full-back, who move at a similar distance from their own goal.

## Random forest

An identical pipeline was used, with a change only in the fourth stage. The
random forest contains two sources of randomness — the sampling of instances
when building each tree and the choice of a subset of features at every split —
so the seed was fixed at 42.

```{r code-rf-grids}
pipe_rf <- base_pipeline %>%
  ml_random_forest_classifier(features_col = "features", label_col = "label",
                              seed = 42)

# S1: ensemble size
g1 <- list(random_forest = list(num_trees = c(20, 50, 100, 250, 500)))
# S2: complexity of an individual tree x strength of decorrelation (sampling COLUMNS)
g2 <- list(random_forest = list(max_depth = c(3, 5, 10, 15),
                                feature_subset_strategy = c("sqrt","log2","onethird")))
# S3: aggressiveness of ROW sampling x pre-pruning
g3 <- list(random_forest = list(subsampling_rate = c(0.6, 0.8, 1.0),
                                min_instances_per_node = c(1, 5, 20)))

t1 <- system.time(cv1 <- run_cv(g1, pipe_rf))
t2 <- system.time(cv2 <- run_cv(g2, pipe_rf))
t3 <- system.time(cv3 <- run_cv(g3, pipe_rf))
```

### Scenario 1 — number of trees in the ensemble

```{r rf-s1, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE}
tab(rf_s1, "Table 10 — Random forest, scenario 1: number of trees")
```

```{r rf-s1-fig, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Figure 14: Random forest, effect of the number of trees"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/RF_S1.png")
```

The largest gain is realised by moving from 20 to 50 trees, where F1 rises by
0.71 percentage points. After that the curve flattens out: a tenfold increase of
the ensemble, from 50 to 500 trees, brings only a further 0.29 percentage
points. The ensemble reduces variance by averaging, with the reduction
proportional to the reciprocal of the number of trees, so the gain falls off
quickly. Unlike depth, increasing the number of trees **does not lead to
overfitting**, which is visible from the absence of a decline in the right-hand
part of the curve.

### Scenario 2 — tree depth and feature subset

The `feature_subset_strategy` parameter determines how many features are
considered at random at **every split**: `sqrt` gives ⌈√29⌉ = 6 features, `log2`
⌈log₂29⌉ = 5, and `onethird` ⌈29/3⌉ = 10. This is column sampling, as opposed to
`subsampling_rate` in the next scenario, which samples rows.

```{r rf-s2, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE}
tab(rf_s2, "Table 11 — Random forest, scenario 2: depth and feature subset")
```

```{r rf-s2-fig, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Figure 15: Random forest, depth and feature selection strategy"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/RF_S2.png")
```

Three regularities stand out. Shallow trees of depth 3 give the worst results
under every strategy, because an individual tree with at most eight leaves
cannot distinguish six classes, so not even averaging removes that limitation.
The `log2` strategy gives the worst results at every depth except the smallest —
with one feature fewer per split it introduces more randomness than is useful.
Finally, `sqrt` peaks at depth 10 and then declines, while `onethird` flattens
out at depths 10 and 15: a smaller subset introduces more diversity, so at large
depths the individual trees overfit more.

### Scenario 3 — subsampling rate and minimum node size

```{r rf-s3, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE}
tab(rf_s3, "Table 12 — Random forest, scenario 3: sampling and node size")
```

```{r rf-s3-fig, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Figure 16: Random forest, subsampling rate and minimum node size"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/RF_S3.png")
```

The influence of both parameters is weak — the total range across all nine
combinations is 1.26 percentage points. A `min_instances_per_node` of 20 gives
the worst results at every subsampling rate, because it stops branching too
early and thereby reduces the diversity among the trees, which is the basic
source of the ensemble's advantage. At the smallest value of the minimum node
size a peak appears at a rate of 0.8, while at larger values F1 rises
monotonically up to 1.0: when the trees are unconstrained in node size, partial
sampling introduces the necessary diversity, whereas with already constrained
trees it only reduces the amount of data.

### Choice of solution and evaluation on the test set

The parameters of the selected model are not transcribed by hand but read from
the model itself and passed to the final training:

```{r code-rf-parameters}
rf_stage <- ml_stage(best_model, 4)
cat("num_trees:",   invoke(spark_jobj(rf_stage), "getNumTrees"), "\n")
cat("max_depth:",   invoke(spark_jobj(rf_stage), "getMaxDepth"), "\n")
cat("subset:",      invoke(spark_jobj(rf_stage), "getFeatureSubsetStrategy"), "\n")
cat("total nodes:", invoke(spark_jobj(rf_stage), "totalNumNodes"), "\n")

pipe_best <- base_pipeline %>%
  ml_random_forest_classifier(
    features_col = "features", label_col = "label", seed = 42,
    num_trees               = invoke(spark_jobj(rf_stage), "getNumTrees"),
    max_depth               = invoke(spark_jobj(rf_stage), "getMaxDepth"),
    feature_subset_strategy = invoke(spark_jobj(rf_stage), "getFeatureSubsetStrategy"),
    subsampling_rate        = invoke(spark_jobj(rf_stage), "getSubsamplingRate"),
    min_instances_per_node  = invoke(spark_jobj(rf_stage), "getMinInstancesPerNode"))

t_fit  <- system.time(final_model <- ml_fit(pipe_best, train))
t_pred <- system.time(ml_transform(final_model, test) %>% sdf_nrow())  # sdf_nrow forces execution
```

The model from the first scenario was chosen: 500 trees, maximum depth 5,
strategy `auto` (which for classification corresponds to the value `sqrt`), a
full subsampling rate and a minimum node size of 1. The ensemble contains 21,544
nodes in total.

The difference between the first and the second scenario is only 0.08 percentage
points, so the results can be considered practically equal. A **limitation of
the search performed** should also be noted: in the first scenario only the
number of trees was varied, with the depth left at its default value of 5, while
the second scenario showed that a depth of 10 is more favourable. The
combination of a large number of trees and a greater depth was not examined,
since the scenarios were, in line with the requirement, defined as separate
units. It is possible that such a combination would give a somewhat better
result.

| Indicator | Value |
|---|---|
| F1 from cross-validation (10 folds) | 0.9244 |
| Accuracy on the test set | 0.9415 |
| 95% confidence interval | (0.911 – 0.964) |
| Cohen's kappa | 0.9284 |
| Macro precision | 0.9513 |
| Macro recall | 0.9448 |
| Macro F1 | 0.9476 |
| Balanced accuracy | 0.9663 |
| Multiclass AUC (Hand–Till) | 0.9966 |
| Training time for a single model | 6.21 s |
| Prediction time over the test set | 0.42 s |
| Total number of nodes in the ensemble | 21,544 |
| Number of models trained in the search | 263 |

*Table 13: Performance indicators of the selected random forest*

The random forest outperforms the decision tree on every indicator. Accuracy is
higher by 2.9 percentage points, macro F1 by 2.5 and kappa by 3.6. The number of
misclassified examples was reduced from 30 to 20, i.e. by a third.

The difference in the AUC indicator is particularly pronounced, rising from
0.9776 to 0.9966. Since that indicator is computed from the distribution of
probabilities, its increase shows that the ensemble not only makes more accurate
decisions but also makes them with a better-calibrated degree of confidence —
the probabilities arise from averaging the predictions of 500 trees, so they are
graded far more finely than the probabilities of a single tree, which are
limited by the composition of the leaves.

The price of that improvement is 2.4 times longer training and a 653 times more
complex model, from 33 to 21,544 nodes.

```{r rf-by-class, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE}
tab(rf_by_class, "Table 14 — Random forest: performance by positional class")
```

The ordering of the classes by difficulty is unchanged relative to the tree, but
an improvement was achieved in every class without exception. The largest single
advance was achieved in the precision of the central midfielder class, which
rises from 0.8415 to 0.9103: with the tree that class served as a dumping ground
for borderline cases, and with the ensemble the phenomenon is considerably
mitigated.

```{r rf-confusion, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Figure 17: Confusion matrix — random forest"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/RF_confusion.png")
```

The structure of the errors is identical to that of the tree. Nineteen of the 20
errors occur between neighbouring classes, and the only exception is again a
full-back placed among the wingers. **The ensemble did not change the nature of
the errors, only their number.**

The feature importance rankings of the two methods are merged for direct
comparison:

```{r code-rf-imp-comparison}
imp <- spark_jobj(rf_stage) %>% invoke("featureImportances") %>% invoke("toArray")
imp_df <- data.frame(obelezje = feat_cols, znacaj = round(imp, 4)) %>%
  arrange(desc(znacaj))

if (file.exists("results/dt_importance.csv")) {
  dt_imp <- read.csv("results/dt_importance.csv")
  poredjenje <- merge(imp_df, dt_imp, by = "obelezje",
                      suffixes = c("_suma", "_stablo")) %>%
    arrange(desc(znacaj_suma))
  write.csv(poredjenje, "results/importance_poredjenje.csv", row.names = FALSE)
}
```

```{r rf-importance, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Figure 18: Feature importance — random forest"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/RF_importance.png")
```

| Feature | Random forest | Decision tree |
|---|---|---|
| `d3_share` | 0.1371 | 0.0702 |
| `mean_x` | 0.1315 | **0.6028** |
| `f3_share` | 0.1232 | 0.0065 |
| `sd_x` | 0.0973 | 0.1218 |
| `clearances_p90` | 0.0802 | **0.0000** |
| `sd_y` | 0.0547 | **0.0000** |
| `tackles_p90` | 0.0347 | **0.0000** |

| `pressures_p90` | 0.0328 | 0.0146 |
