| `carries_p90` | 0.0226 | 0.0278 |

*Table 15: Feature importance — random forest versus decision tree*

The comparison reveals a fundamental difference in the way the two methods use
the features. In the tree the importance is markedly concentrated: `mean_x`
carries 60.3%, and the first four features 89.6%. In the forest the distribution
is considerably more even: the most important feature carries 13.7%, and the
first four 48.9%.

The cause lies in the random selection of a subset of features. The feature
`mean_x` is not available at most splits, so the tree has to fall back on
related features. The consequence is most noticeable for four features —
`clearances_p90`, `sd_y`, `tackles_p90` and `miscontrols_p90` — which the
selected tree did not use even once, while in the ensemble they carry 20.2% of
the importance between them.

The importance ordering in the forest is considerably closer to the results of
the analysis of variance than the ordering from the tree, which is to be
expected: the analysis of variance measures the individual discriminative power
of each feature independently of the others, and it is precisely such a measure
that the ensemble approximates better. The practical conclusion is that feature
importance in a single tree should be interpreted with caution in the presence
of correlated features.

## The k-nearest-neighbours method

Spark is used here only to load the identical split, after which the connection
is closed — the 1360 × 29 training matrix fits entirely in memory, so keeping
the executors alive during the long R phase would be spending 8 GB with no
benefit.

So that the numbers remain comparable with the Spark pipelines, the weighted F1
measure was implemented with a definition **identical** to the one in
`MulticlassClassificationEvaluator(metric_name = "f1")`:

```{r code-knn-f1}
f1_weighted <- function(actual, predicted, levels_ = lvl) {
  tab  <- table(factor(predicted, levels = levels_),
                factor(actual,    levels = levels_))   # rows: predictions
  tp   <- diag(tab)
  prec <- tp / rowSums(tab)          # denominator: how many times the class was predicted
  rec  <- tp / colSums(tab)          # denominator: how many times the class occurs
  f1   <- 2 * prec * rec / (prec + rec)
  f1[!is.finite(f1)] <- 0            # a class that is neither predicted nor present
  w    <- colSums(tab) / sum(tab)    # weights by the frequency of the true class
  sum(w * f1)
}
```

Standardisation is, as in the pipeline, learned **exclusively on the training
part of each fold**; the built-in scaling in `kknn` is switched off because it
would do it over the whole dataset:

```{r code-knn-scale}
scale_pair <- function(A, B) {
  m <- colMeans(A); s <- apply(A, 2, stats::sd)
  s[s == 0 | is.na(s)] <- 1
  list(A = scale(A, center = m, scale = s),
       B = scale(B, center = m, scale = s))
}

knn_predict <- function(Xa, ya, Xb, yb, k, distance, kernel) {
  dtr <- data.frame(Xa, y = ya, check.names = FALSE)
  dte <- data.frame(Xb, y = yb, check.names = FALSE)
  kknn::kknn(y ~ ., train = dtr, test = dte,
             k = k, distance = distance, kernel = kernel,
             scale = FALSE)          # we have already done the scaling ourselves
}
```

The cross-validation was written by hand, with **stratified** folds, so the
results of all ten folds were kept and the standard deviation, which
`ml_validation_metrics` does not return, is therefore available:

```{r code-knn-cv}
set.seed(42)
folds <- caret::createFolds(ytr, k = 10, list = TRUE, returnTrain = FALSE)

cv_knn <- function(k, distance = 2, kernel = "rectangular") {
  vapply(folds, function(idx) {
    s   <- scale_pair(Xtr[-idx, , drop = FALSE], Xtr[idx, , drop = FALSE])
    fit <- knn_predict(s$A, ytr[-idx], s$B, ytr[idx], k, distance, kernel)
    f1_weighted(ytr[idx], fit$fitted.values)
  }, numeric(1))
}

run_grid <- function(grid) {
  bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(nrow(grid)), function(i) {
    f1s <- cv_knn(grid$k[i], grid$distance[i], grid$kernel[i])
    cbind(grid[i, , drop = FALSE],
          f1    = round(mean(f1s), 4),
          f1_sd = round(stats::sd(f1s), 4),
          f1_se = round(stats::sd(f1s) / sqrt(length(f1s)), 4))
  }))
}

g1 <- expand.grid(k = c(1,3,5,7,9,11,15,21,31,51),
                  distance = 2, kernel = "rectangular", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
g2 <- expand.grid(k = c(5,9,15,21,31), distance = 2,
                  kernel = c("rectangular","triangular","gaussian","inv"),
                  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
g3 <- expand.grid(k = c(5,9,15,21,31), distance = c(1,2,3),
                  kernel = "rectangular", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
```

KNN is a lazy classifier: there is no training phase in the proper sense, the
model is the training set itself, and all the computation is deferred to the
moment of prediction.

### Scenario 1 — number of neighbours

```{r knn-s1, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE}
tab(knn_s1, "Table 16 — KNN, scenario 1: number of neighbours")
```

```{r knn-s1-fig, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Figure 19: KNN, effect of the number of neighbours (error bars are ±1 SE)"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/KNN_S1.png")
```

For k = 1 the model memorises individual instances and F1 drops to 0.8789 — that
is the only configuration that stands out convincingly from the rest. From k = 5
onwards the curve flattens and stays in the band 0.917–0.923 all the way to
k = 51, where slight over-smoothing of the boundaries begins to reduce the
result. It is also observed that the standard deviation across folds decreases
monotonically as k grows (0.0321 for k = 5 versus 0.0160 for k = 21), which is a
direct consequence of averaging over more neighbours.

### Scenario 2 — weighting the neighbours' votes

```{r knn-s2, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE}
tab(knn_s2, "Table 17 — KNN, scenario 2: kernel function")
```

```{r knn-s2-fig, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Figure 20: KNN, the way the neighbours' votes are weighted"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/KNN_S2.png")
```

The structure of the results is instructive: **weighting helps only at large k.**
For k = 5 the triangular kernel is the worst in the whole scenario (0.9045),
because with few neighbours an aggressive reduction of the weight of the most
distant ones effectively reduces the decision to two or three votes and brings
back an instability similar to the one at k = 1. At k = 31 the same kernel
becomes the best (0.9261), because it damps the contribution of distant
neighbours that no longer belong to the local neighbourhood.

### Scenario 3 — distance metric

```{r knn-s3, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE}
tab(knn_s3, "Table 18 — KNN, scenario 3: Minkowski parameter")
```

```{r knn-s3-fig, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Figure 21: KNN, effect of the distance metric"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/KNN_S3.png")
```

This is the scenario with the most pronounced influence. The Manhattan distance
is the best at larger k (0.9292 for k = 21), while p = 3 is consistently the
weakest at all five points. The explanation lies in the dimensionality of the
space: with 29 standardised features, a larger p increasingly allows a single
feature with a large deviation to dominate the distance, so the neighbourhood is
determined on the basis of an exception rather than on the basis of the player's
overall profile. The Manhattan metric sums the absolute deviations evenly and is
therefore more robust.

### Choice of solution and evaluation on the test set

The chosen configuration is **k = 21, Manhattan distance (p = 1), unweighted
voting**, with CV F1 = 0.9292 (SE = 0.0079).

The choice should be interpreted with a caveat. The total range across all 45
configurations examined is 0.8789–0.9292, and the typical standard error across
folds is 0.0071. The difference between the best results of the three scenarios
(0.9232, 0.9261, 0.9292) is smaller than one standard error, so it cannot be
claimed that the chosen configuration is statistically significantly better than
a dozen others. The only findings that rise above the noise are the weakness of
k = 1 and the systematic advantage of the Manhattan metric over p = 3.

| Indicator | Value |
|---|---|
| F1 from cross-validation (10 folds) | 0.9292 |
| Accuracy on the test set | 0.9357 |
| 95% confidence interval | (0.904 – 0.959) |
| Cohen's kappa | 0.9214 |
| Weighted F1 on the test set | 0.9359 |
| Macro precision | 0.9398 |
| Macro recall | 0.9447 |
| Macro F1 | 0.9416 |
| Balanced accuracy | 0.9658 |
| Multiclass AUC (Hand–Till) | 0.9962 |
| Preparation of the reference set | 0.11 s |
| Prediction time over the test set | 0.32 s |
| Number of models evaluated in the search | 451 |

*Table 19: Performance indicators of the selected KNN model*

```{r knn-by-class, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE}
tab(knn_by_class, "Table 20 — KNN: performance by positional class")
```

```{r knn-confusion, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Figure 22: Confusion matrix — KNN"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/KNN_confusion.png")
```

Of the 22 errors in total, nine fall on the AM_W–FW pair. That is also the only
pair with two-way confusion and it explains why FW has the lowest precision
(0.857) and AM_W the lowest recall (0.889). The error is not technical but
substantive: in modern formations a winger who frequently cuts inside into the
penalty area and a wide forward have an almost identical profile of touches,
runs and spatial distribution.

An AUC of 0.9962 is high, but it should be read with care: with an unweighted
kernel the probabilities are multiples of 1/21, so the resolution of the ranking
is coarse and the measure is less informative than for methods that produce
smooth probabilities.

The cost profile is characteristic of lazy learning: "training" takes 0.11 s
because it amounts to forming the reference table, while prediction takes three
times longer even though it concerns a set that is four times smaller. For the
tree and the forest the relation is reversed. The relation of the times per
scenario is also interesting: S1, with only 10 combinations, takes 15.8 s, while
S2, with 20 combinations, takes 6.7 s, because S1 contains k = 51 and the
complexity of the neighbour search grows with k. **For KNN the number of
combinations is not a good indicator of cost** — what matters is the value of k
and the number of instances.

KNN has no built-in importance measure, so **permutation importance** was
applied: every feature is randomly shuffled in the test set and the drop in the
weighted F1 measure is measured:

```{r code-knn-imp}
set.seed(42); REPS <- 5
base_f1 <- f1_weighted(yte, final$fitted.values)

drops <- vapply(seq_along(feat_cols), function(j) {
  mean(replicate(REPS, {
    Xp <- s_full$B
    Xp[, j] <- sample(Xp[, j])            # shuffle only the j-th feature
    fp <- knn_predict(s_full$A, ytr, Xp, yte,
                      best_row$k, best_row$distance, best_row$kernel)
    base_f1 - f1_weighted(yte, fp$fitted.values)
  }))
}, numeric(1))
```

```{r knn-importance, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Figure 23: Feature importance — KNN (permutation)"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/KNN_importance.png")
```

Two spatial features dominate: `mean_y` carries 19% of the total drop, and
`sd_x` a further 16%.

Two caveats on the interpretation. First, this is not the same scale as the Gini
importance for the tree and the forest, which by definition sums to 1 — the
ordering is comparable, not the absolute value. Second, **permutation importance
underestimates features that are correlated with one another**: if two features
carry the same information, shuffling one does no harm because the other remains
untouched, so both appear unimportant. That is precisely what explains why
`mean_y` is in first place even though by the analysis of variance it is not
even among the top five — it has no strong correlate in the dataset, so
shuffling it cannot be compensated for.

## Choice of solution across all methods

### Selection criterion

The choice was guided by the F1 measure from cross-validation, i.e. by the same
criterion applied when selecting the parameters within each method. The test set
was not used as a selection criterion but exclusively as independent
confirmation. Where the values were approximately equal, supplementary criteria
were applied — the structure of the errors, the cost of prediction, the
behaviour as the data volume grows and the interpretability of the model.

Since all three scripts write a row with **identical column names**, the
comparison reduces to merging three files:

```{r code-comparison}
paths <- c(KNN = "results/knn_best.csv",
           DT  = "results/dt_best.csv",
           RF  = "results/rf_best.csv")
existing <- paths[file.exists(paths)]

svi <- bind_rows(lapply(existing, read.csv)) %>% arrange(desc(cv_f1))
winner <- svi$metod[which.max(svi$cv_f1)]

svi %>%
  select(metod, cv_f1, test_tacnost, makro_f1, bal_tacnost) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-metod, names_to = "pokazatelj", values_to = "vrednost") %>%
  ggplot(aes(pokazatelj, vrednost, fill = metod)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.8, 1.0)) +
  labs(title = "Comparison of the classification methods",
       subtitle = "CV F1 from the training set, everything else from the test set",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Method")
ggsave("figures/POREDJENJE_metode.png", width = 8, height = 4.5, dpi = 150)
```

```{r comparison-table, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE}
tab(comparison, "Table 21 — Comparison of all three classification methods")
```


### Comparison by cross-validation

| Method | CV F1 | Difference from the best |
|---|---|---|
| KNN | 0.9292 | — |
| Random forest | 0.9244 | −0.0048 |
| Decision tree | 0.8857 | −0.0435 |

*Table 22: Comparison by the F1 measure from cross-validation*

The comparison separates two clearly distinct situations.

**The decision tree lags behind by more than four percentage points.** The
difference is several times larger than the standard error across folds, which
is approximately 0.007, so the finding is unambiguous.

**The difference between KNN and the random forest cannot be considered real.**
There are two reasons for this. The first is statistical: 0.0048 is less than
one standard error, so the intervals overlap. The second is methodological —
although an identical definition of the weighted F1 measure was deliberately
applied for KNN, the two values **did not arise over the same folds**. For the
tree and the forest the folds are formed by `ml_cross_validator` without
stratification, for KNN by `caret::createFolds` with stratification. Comparing
differences on the order of thousandths between two different folding schemes is
not justified.

The primary criterion therefore separates the tree from the other two methods,
but **does not separate the random forest from KNN.**

### Comparison on the test set

| Indicator | Tree | Random forest | KNN |
|---|---|---|---|
| Accuracy | 0.9123 | **0.9415** | 0.9357 |
| 95% confidence interval | 0.877–0.940 | 0.911–0.964 | 0.904–0.959 |
| Cohen's kappa | 0.8926 | **0.9284** | 0.9214 |
| Weighted F1 | 0.9131 | **0.9417** | 0.9359 |
| Macro precision | 0.9276 | **0.9513** | 0.9398 |
| Macro recall | 0.9191 | **0.9448** | 0.9447 |
| Macro F1 | 0.9226 | **0.9476** | 0.9416 |
| Balanced accuracy | 0.9504 | **0.9663** | 0.9658 |
| Multiclass AUC | 0.9776 | **0.9966** | 0.9962 |
| Number of errors (out of 342) | 30 | **20** | 22 |

*Table 23: Comparison on the independent test set*

The values of the weighted F1 measure on the test set were derived from the
per-class F1 measures and the number of instances per class, in order to compare
them with the measure from cross-validation, which is also weighted.

**The ordering has reversed relative to cross-validation.** The random forest is
better than KNN on all nine indicators, whereas in cross-validation it was
second. The reversal is not in itself unusual — the test set comprises 342
instances, so a difference of two misclassified instances shifts the accuracy by
0.6 percentage points, and the confidence intervals overlap to a large extent.
What is significant is the **consistency**: the forest is not better on average
with random exceptions, but on every single indicator.

| Class | Tree | Random forest | KNN |
|---|---|---|---|
| GK | 1.0000 | 1.0000 | 1.0000 |
| CB | 0.9655 | **0.9744** | 0.9587 |
| FB | 0.9385 | **0.9630** | 0.9538 |
| DM_CM | 0.8846 | **0.9342** | 0.9324 |
| AM_W | 0.8630 | 0.8966 | **0.9014** |
| FW | 0.8837 | **0.9176** | 0.9032 |

*Table 24: F1 measure by positional class, all three methods*

Of the five non-trivial classes the random forest is the best in four, and KNN
in one.

### The structure of the errors — a shared ceiling

| Class pair | Tree | Random forest | KNN |
|---|---|---|---|
| AM_W – FW | 10 | 7 | 9 |
| DM_CM – AM_W | 9 | 7 | 4 |
| FB – DM_CM | 6 | 2 | 3 |
| CB – DM_CM | 3 | 1 | 3 |
| CB – FB | 1 | 2 | 2 |
| FB – AM_W | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| **Total** | **30** | **20** | **22** |

*Table 25: Distribution of the errors by class pair*

This is the most informative part of the comparison. **All three methods make
their errors in the same places.** Two pairs — wingers and forwards, and central
and attacking midfielders — carry 63% of the errors for the tree, 70% for the
forest and 59% for KNN. No method has a single error between classes at opposite
ends of the defence–attack spectrum, and the goalkeeper class is left without a
single error in all three cases.

Three methods with fundamentally different inductive approaches — a single tree
of rules, an ensemble of 500 trees and a distance-based method in a 29-dimensional
space — produce **the same structure of errors.** If it were a matter of a
capacity shortfall of an individual method, the distribution of the errors would
differ. The consistency shows that the limit lies in the data itself, which is
entirely consistent with the prediction from the principal component plot.

The differences between the methods come down to how close they are to that
shared ceiling. The tree is the furthest away. The forest and KNN are
practically on it, with the forest separating wingers from forwards better (7
versus 9), and KNN separating central from attacking midfielders better (4
versus 7).

### Comparison of feature importance

```{r imp-all, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE}
tab(imp_all, "Table 26 — Feature importance across all three methods")
```

The three methods give three different rankings, and the differences are a
consequence of the construction of the measures themselves. The random forest
gives the list closest to the analysis of variance, the tree the most distorted
one (60.3% in a single feature), and KNN a third one, different again, because
the permutation measure underestimates correlated features. The common finding,
despite the differences in ordering, is that **spatial features dominate in all
three methods.**

### Cost and behaviour as the data volume grows

| Quantity | Tree | Random forest | KNN |
|---|---|---|---|
| Training a single model | 2.60 s | 6.21 s | 0.11 s |
| Prediction over 342 instances | 0.50 s | 0.42 s | 0.32 s |
| Number of models in the search | 273 | 263 | 451 |
| Model size | 33 nodes | 21,544 nodes | 1360 × 29 matrix |
| Environment | Spark MLlib | Spark MLlib | R, `kknn` |

*Table 27: The cost of training and prediction*

The most important difference for practical use is not visible from the measured
values, because a set of 1,702 players is too small to expose it. **The cost of
prediction for KNN grows linearly with the size of the training set**, since for
every new instance the distance to all 1,360 reference points has to be
computed. For the tree and the forest the cost of prediction **does not depend
on the size of the training set** — it is determined by the number of trees and
their depth. In addition, KNN has to keep the entire training set as its model;
there is no compression of what has been learned into a more compact form.

### The selected solution

> **As the final solution across all methods, the random forest with 500 trees,
> a maximum depth of 5 and the `sqrt` strategy for selecting the feature subset
> was chosen.**

The rationale, step by step:

1. **The decision tree was ruled out on the basis of cross-validation.** A
   shortfall of 0.0435 exceeds the standard error several times over and was
   confirmed on the test set, where the tree makes 50% more errors.
2. **Cross-validation did not separate the forest from KNN**, so the primary
   criterion gives no answer and supplementary criteria are applied.
3. **Consistency on the independent test set** — the forest is better on all
   nine indicators and in four of the five non-trivial classes.
4. **Behaviour as the data volume grows** — the cost of prediction for the
   forest does not depend on the size of the training set, whereas for KNN it
   grows linearly. For a project set up over gigabytes of data this is a
   decisive property.
5. **Interpretability** — the forest gives a feature importance measure
   consistent with the analysis of variance, whereas the permutation-based
   substitute for KNN proved distorted in the presence of correlated features.
6. **Quality of the probability estimates** — the forest gives smoothly graded
   probabilities, whereas for KNN they are multiples of 1/21.

### Limitations of the choice

The cross-validation folds are not identical for all three methods. Repeating
the whole procedure over common, pre-fixed folds would remove this uncertainty
and enable a paired comparison across folds, which is a considerably more
sensitive procedure than comparing means.

For the tree and the forest only the means across folds are available, since
`ml_validation_metrics` does not return the dispersion. Confidence intervals
from cross-validation were therefore computed only for KNN.

The test set comprises 342 instances, so one misclassified instance changes the
accuracy by 0.29 percentage points. The two-instance difference between the
forest and KNN lies within that sensitivity.

The parameter search was carried out by scenarios, as separate units, so none of
the three solutions is necessarily the best possible one for that method.

# Clustering

## Setup

Clustering is an unsupervised, descriptive procedure: the goal is not prediction
but the description of a structure that exists in the data independently of the
positional labels. What is grouped are the **instances**, i.e. the rows of the
player-level table, not the features.

The **k-means method** was applied, a representative of partitional clustering.
Every player belongs to exactly one cluster, a cluster is represented by its
centroid, and membership is determined by the Euclidean distance from the
centroid.

The choice of method was guided by computational complexity. The k-means method
has complexity O(k·s·t), i.e. linear in the number of entities, while
hierarchical clustering is between O(s² log s) and O(s³), and density-based
clustering O(s log s). At the data volume this project was set up for, only the
k-means method remains directly applicable and it is the only one with a
distributed implementation in the Spark MLlib library.

Unlike the k-nearest-neighbours method, where the Minkowski parameter was the
subject of the third scenario, here the dissimilarity measure **is not a free
parameter**: the method is defined via the Euclidean distance, since the
centroid is computed as the arithmetic mean of the members. The metric therefore
cannot be a scenario.

The analysis was carried out over the **entire set of 1,702 players.** The split
into a training and a test part was formed for the sake of classification and
serves no purpose in an unsupervised procedure.

```{r code-km-loading}
train <- spark_read_parquet(sc, "train", sp("data/interim/train"))
test  <- spark_read_parquet(sc, "test",  sp("data/interim/test"))
dat   <- sdf_bind_rows(train, test)          # the whole dataset: 1702 players

dat_r <- dat %>% select(all_of(c(feat_cols, "position_group"))) %>% collect()
Xraw  <- as.matrix(dat_r[, feat_cols])
poz   <- factor(dat_r$position_group, levels = lvl)   # ONLY for interpretation

Xs <- scale(Xraw, center = TRUE, scale = TRUE)
```

Centring and scaling resolve the method's well-known sensitivity to feature
scale: without them `passes_p90`, of the order of tens, would dominate the
distance over shares in the range from 0 to 1. The Euclidean distance over
standardised data is equivalent to the standardised Euclidean distance over the
original values.

Two feature spaces are prepared by separate pipelines. PCA is applied **to the
standardised** data, since `ft_pca` does not centre on its own:

```{r code-km-pipelines}
prep_std <- ml_pipeline(sc) %>%
  ft_vector_assembler(input_cols = feat_cols, output_col = "features_raw") %>%
  ft_standard_scaler("features_raw", "features", with_mean = TRUE, with_std = TRUE)

prep_pca <- ml_pipeline(sc) %>%
  ft_vector_assembler(input_cols = feat_cols, output_col = "features_raw") %>%
  ft_standard_scaler("features_raw", "features_std", with_mean = TRUE, with_std = TRUE) %>%
  ft_pca(input_col = "features_std", output_col = "features", k = 11)

tbl_std <- ml_transform(ml_fit(prep_std, dat), dat)
tbl_pca <- ml_transform(ml_fit(prep_pca, dat), dat)
```

Two quantities were used as quality measures.

**Within-cluster variability W(C)**, defined as the sum of squared Euclidean
distances over all ordered pairs of entities within a cluster, divided by the
number of members. The identity W(C) = 2·SSE(C) holds, because

$$\sum_{i,j \in C} \lVert x_i - x_j \rVert^2 = 2\,\lvert C\rvert \sum_{i \in C} \lVert x_i - c \rVert^2 .$$

```{r code-km-w}
sse <- function(X, cl) {
  sum(vapply(unique(cl), function(g) {
    Xi <- X[cl == g, , drop = FALSE]
    if (nrow(Xi) < 2) return(0)
    sum(sweep(Xi, 2, colMeans(Xi))^2)
  }, numeric(1)))
}
W_ukupno <- function(X, cl) 2 * sse(X, cl)

# checking the identity: over all pairs versus over deviations from the centroid
provera_W <- function(Xi) {
  d2    <- as.matrix(dist(Xi))^2
  W_par <- 2 * sum(d2[upper.tri(d2)]) / nrow(Xi)
  W_sse <- 2 * sum(sweep(Xi, 2, colMeans(Xi))^2)
  c(preko_parova = W_par, preko_sse = W_sse)
}
```

The identity was checked numerically over the goalkeeper cluster: 1,806 both
ways.

**The silhouette coefficient** is computed with the `ml_clustering_evaluator`
object. The adjusted Rand index and the purity measure were also computed, but
**were not used as a selection criterion** — both rely on the positional labels,
so using them when choosing the number of clusters would turn the procedure into
a supervised one:

```{r code-km-measures}
evaluator_sil <- ml_clustering_evaluator(
  sc, features_col = "features", prediction_col = "prediction",
  metric_name = "silhouette")

cistoca <- function(cl, klase) {              # purity
  tab <- table(cl, klase); sum(apply(tab, 1, max)) / sum(tab)
}

ari <- function(cl, klase) {                 # adjusted Rand index
  tab <- table(cl, klase); n <- sum(tab)
  c2 <- function(x) x * (x - 1) / 2
  suma_ij <- sum(c2(tab)); suma_i <- sum(c2(rowSums(tab)))
  suma_j  <- sum(c2(colSums(tab)))
  ocek <- suma_i * suma_j / c2(n)
  (suma_ij - ocek) / (0.5 * (suma_i + suma_j) - ocek)
}

oceni_k <- function(tbl, X, k, oznaka, init_mode = "k-means||", seed = 42) {
  model <- ml_kmeans(tbl, formula = NULL, k = k, features_col = "features",
                     init_mode = init_mode, max_iter = 50, seed = seed)
  tr <- ml_transform(model, tbl)
  pr <- tr %>% select(prediction) %>% collect() %>% pull(prediction)
  data.frame(prostor = oznaka, k = k,
             W = round(W_ukupno(X, pr), 1), SSE = round(sse(X, pr), 1),
             silueta = round(ml_evaluate(evaluator_sil, tr), 4),
             najmanji = min(table(pr)), najveci = max(table(pr)),
             cistoca = round(cistoca(pr, poz), 4),
             ari = round(ari(pr, poz), 4))
}
```

## Scenario 1 — number of clusters

The number of clusters is the only parameter the method requires in advance, and
that is its well-known drawback. Nine values were examined, from 2 to 10.

```{r code-km-s1}
K_RANGE <- 2:10
vm1 <- bind_rows(lapply(K_RANGE, function(k) oceni_k(tbl_std, Xs, k, "29 obelezja")))

# relative drop in W — a numerical complement to the visual elbow rule
vm1 <- vm1 %>% mutate(pad_W = round(c(NA, -diff(W)) / lag(W) * 100, 1))
```

```{r km-s1, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE}
tab(km_s1, "Table 28 — k-means, scenario 1: number of clusters")
```

```{r km-s1-fig, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Figure 25: k-means, the elbow method and the silhouette coefficient"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/KM_S1.png")
```

**Both criteria point to the same value.** The elbow method: the drop in
within-cluster variability is 26.8% when moving from two to three clusters, then
12.9%, then 9.4%, and from there on it stays below six per cent. The elbow is
clearly pronounced at **k = 3**. The silhouette coefficient independently
reaches its maximum at the same value, 0.4760, with the second-best value being
0.3850.

The agreement of the two criteria is significant, since they measure different
things: the elbow assesses cluster compactness, the silhouette the relation
between compactness and separation. On the usual interpretation scale a value of
0.4760 falls in the range of a weak but existing structure, which is a fair
expectation for a dataset in which five of the six positional classes form a
continuum.

It is also observed that the smallest cluster has exactly 125 members at every
value of k from 3 to 8 — as many as there are goalkeepers in the dataset.

## Scenario 2 — feature space

The pair `d3_share`–`mean_x` has a correlation coefficient of −0.980. In
distance-based methods redundant features count the same information more than
once and thereby implicitly weight it, changing the dissimilarity measure
itself. The same range of k values was examined over 11 principal components,
which carry 90.35% of the total variance and are orthogonal by construction.

```{r code-km-s2}
Xp <- prcomp(Xs, center = FALSE, scale. = FALSE)$x[, 1:11]
vm2_pca <- bind_rows(lapply(K_RANGE, function(k) oceni_k(tbl_pca, Xp, k, "11 komponenti")))
vm2 <- bind_rows(vm1 %>% select(-pad_W), vm2_pca)
```

```{r km-s2, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE}
tab(km_s2, "Table 29 — k-means, scenario 2: comparison of the feature spaces")
```

```{r km-s2-fig, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Figure 26: k-means, comparison of the two feature spaces"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/KM_S2.png")
```

**A note on the comparison:** the absolute values of W and SSE **are not
comparable between the two spaces**, because 11 components contain only 90.35%
of the total variance, so the total variability to be explained is also smaller.
What is comparable is the normalised share of explained variability,
1 − SSE(k)/SSE(1), where SSE(1) = 49,329 for the space of all features and
44,569 for the space of components. At k = 3 that is 46.0% versus 50.8%. The
silhouette coefficient and the Rand index are dimensionless and directly
comparable.

The finding is twofold.

**Dimensionality reduction improves the quality of the partition.** The
silhouette coefficient is higher in the space of components at all nine values
of k, on average by 0.04. The explanation is precisely the one predicted in the
section on correlations: by removing redundancy, every independent dimension of
variability enters the distance exactly once.

**The reduction does not change what the clusters capture.** At k = 3 the purity
is identical (0.4636 in both cases), and the Rand index practically the same
(0.3465 versus 0.3450). The structure is the same, only more clearly delineated
in the space of components.

Both spaces independently select k = 3, which confirms the choice from the first
scenario.

## Stability of the solution

The k-means method converges to a local optimum and is sensitive to the initial
configuration, so several runs with different initial states are recommended.

```{r code-km-stability}
stabilnost <- bind_rows(lapply(c("k-means||", "random"), function(im) {
  bind_rows(lapply(c(1, 7, 42, 2024, 31337), function(s) {
    r <- oceni_k(tbl_std, Xs, 3, "29 obelezja", init_mode = im, seed = s)
    data.frame(init = im, seme = s, W = r$W, silueta = r$silueta, ari = r$ari)
  }))
}))
```

```{r km-stab, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE}
tab(km_stab, "Table 30 — Stability check of the solution at k = 3")
```

The range of the W values across all ten runs is **0.1**, and the range of the
silhouette coefficient **0.0002**. The initialisation method made no difference.
The solution is therefore completely stable and is not trapped in a poor local
optimum.

## The selected solution and the structure of the clusters

**Three clusters over the space of all 29 standardised features** were selected.
The number of clusters was confirmed three times over: by the elbow method, by
the silhouette coefficient and by independent repetition in the space of
principal components. The space of all features was retained for the structural
analysis, even though the silhouette is higher in the space of components
(0.5174 versus 0.4760), for the sake of interpretability — centroids in the
space of the original features have a direct footballing meaning.

```{r code-km-final}
model <- ml_kmeans(tbl_std, formula = NULL, k = 3, features_col = "features",
                   init_mode = "k-means||", max_iter = 50, seed = 42)

klaster <- ml_transform(model, tbl_std) %>%
  select(prediction) %>% collect() %>% pull(prediction)
klaster <- factor(paste0("C", klaster + 1))     # C1..C3 instead of 0..2

ukrstena <- table(klaster, poz)                 # only now are the positions used
```

```{r km-best, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE}
if (!is.null(km_best)) {
  km_best |>
    select(-any_of(c("silueta", "udeo_negativne"))) |>
    tab("Table 31 — Indicators of the selected solution")
}
```

| Cluster | Number of members | GK | CB | FB | DM_CM | AM_W | FW |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| C1 | 125 | **125** | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| C2 | 966 | 0 | **300** | **325** | **320** | 21 | 0 |
| C3 | 611 | 0 | 0 | 7 | 48 | **339** | **217** |

*Table 32: The relation between the clusters and the positional classes*

The purity is 0.4636 and the adjusted Rand index 0.3465. Both values appear low
at first glance and, taken on their own, would lead to the wrong conclusion. The
table shows the opposite.

**No position is scattered across the clusters:**

| Class | Dominant cluster | Share in it |
|---|---|---|
| GK | C1 | 100.0% |
| CB | C2 | 100.0% |
| FB | C2 | 97.9% |
| DM_CM | C2 | 87.0% |
| AM_W | C3 | 94.2% |
| FW | C3 | 100.0% |

*Table 33: Coverage of the positional classes by the dominant cluster*

If the clusters are interpreted as supergroups — C1 goalkeepers, C2 the defence
and the midfield, C3 the attack — then **1,626 of the 1,702 players, i.e. 95.5%,
belong to the cluster corresponding to their supergroup.**

Low purity therefore does not mean disagreement but **the coarseness of the
partition.** For each cluster the purity measure takes the share of the most
numerous class only, so cluster C2, which contains three positional classes in
roughly equal measure (CB 31.1%, FB 33.6%, DM_CM 33.1%), receives a score of
just 33.6% even though it contains no foreign element other than 21 attacking
midfielders. The same holds for the Rand index, which penalises the merging of
classes even when the merging is entirely consistent.

The essential finding is that **the unsupervised procedure discovers three
supergroups rather than six positions, and that those supergroups are nested
within the positional ordering without crossing it.** The boundary between C2
and C3 runs between the central and the attacking midfielders, i.e. in the
middle of the defence–attack spectrum.

```{r km-pca-clusters, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Figure 27: The clusters in the space of the principal components"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/KM_pca_klasteri.png")
```

```{r km-pca-positions, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Figure 28: The same points coloured by positional class"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/KM_pca_pozicije.png")
```

A comparison of the two figures shows most directly what the clusters capture:
the arrangement of the points is the same, and the colours differ only in that
the clustering merges neighbouring positional classes into supergroups.

The relation between the silhouette and the Rand index expresses the same thing
numerically. The silhouette coefficient, an unsupervised measure, has its
maximum at k = 3. The adjusted Rand index, which measures agreement with the
positions, has its maximum at **k = 7** (0.6598), where the purity reaches
0.8719. **Agreement with the positional labels requires more clusters than the
density structure offers.** The two curves have their maxima in different
places, and that divergence is the main quantitative result of this part.

```{r km-silhouette, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Figure 29: Silhouette profile of the selected solution"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/KM_silueta.png")
```

The goalkeeper cluster has a markedly high mean silhouette, while C2 and C3 are
considerably lower — as expected, since they share a boundary that is not sharp
in the data. The share of instances with a negative silhouette is below one per
cent, which means that almost no player is obviously misplaced.

## The relation between feature values and cluster membership

Which features determine the partition is established by a one-way analysis of
variance with the cluster as the factor, and the profile is displayed as a heat
map of the centroids:

```{r code-km-profiles}
f_vred <- vapply(feat_cols, function(f)
  summary(aov(Xs[, f] ~ klaster))[[1]][["F value"]][1], numeric(1))
f_df <- data.frame(obelezje = names(f_vred), F_vrednost = round(f_vred, 1)) %>%
  arrange(desc(F_vrednost))

centroidi <- as.data.frame(t(sapply(levels(klaster), function(g)
  colMeans(Xs[klaster == g, , drop = FALSE]))))
centroidi$klaster <- rownames(centroidi)

top_f <- head(f_df$obelezje, 15)
centroidi %>%
  select(klaster, all_of(top_f)) %>%
  pivot_longer(-klaster, names_to = "obelezje", values_to = "z") %>%
  mutate(obelezje = factor(obelezje, levels = rev(top_f))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(klaster, obelezje, fill = z)) +
  geom_tile() + geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f", z)), size = 2.8) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "steelblue4", mid = "white", high = "firebrick",
                       midpoint = 0) +
  labs(title = "Cluster profiles",
       subtitle = "Centroids in standardised units; 0 is the mean of the whole dataset",
       x = "Cluster", y = NULL, fill = "z")
ggsave("figures/KM_centroidi.png", width = 7.5, height = 6.5, dpi = 150)
```

```{r km-features, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE}
if (!is.null(km_features)) {
  km_features |> head(12) |>
    tab("Table 34 — The features that separate the clusters most (ANOVA F)")
}
```

The first six features coincide, in a changed order, with the first seven by
discriminative power with respect to position. The groups the algorithm found
are therefore not defined by some hidden feature, but by the very same
quantities that separate the positions as well — only more coarsely.

In first place is `avg_pass_length`, a feature that the selected decision tree
did not use even once, because in the presence of `mean_x` it was redundant.
Here it is the strongest, because clustering does not choose one feature per
split but uses all of them simultaneously through the Euclidean distance.
Goalkeepers with their long clearances and forwards with short passes in tight
spaces lie at opposite ends of that axis.

```{r km-centroids-fig, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Figure 30: Cluster profiles — centroids in standardised units"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/KM_centroidi.png")
```

The cluster profile has a clear structure along two axes.

**The spatial axis** separates all three clusters: `mean_x`, `d3_share` and
`f3_share` change sign and magnitude from C1 through C2 to C3, following the
shift of the centre of gravity from one's own goal towards the opposition goal.

**The axis of risk in possession** separates mainly C2 from C3. The features
`miscontrols_p90` and `dispossessed_p90` are high on the list, above
`shots_p90`. Players in the attacking third lose the ball considerably more
often, because they receive it under pressure, in tight spaces and with their
back to goal. That is a feature of behaviour rather than of position, and it
constitutes a second independent source of separation.

```{r km-centroids-table, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE}
if (!is.null(km_centroids)) {
  km_centroids |>
    select(any_of(c("klaster", "n", "mean_x", "d3_share", "f3_share",
                    "avg_pass_length", "miscontrols_p90", "shots_p90"))) |>
    tab("Table 35 — Centroids in the original units (selected features)", digits = 2)
}
```

```{r km-composition, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Figure 31: Composition of the clusters by positional class"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/KM_sastav.png")
```

```{r km-boxplot, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Figure 32: Distribution of the features across the clusters"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/KM_boxplot.png")
```

The box plots in the original units confirm that the separation is not the
consequence of individual outlying values but of a shift of whole distributions.

# Conclusion

5,321,459 events from 1,517 matches in four European leagues were analysed,
aggregated into a player-level table with 1,702 rows and 29 numeric features.

**Spatial features determine position.** The analysis of variance showed that
the strongest spatial feature has 5.6 times the discriminative power of the
strongest event counter. The same finding is confirmed independently by all
three classification methods through their feature importance measures, and by
the clustering as well. A player's position is read more reliably from where the
player moves than from which actions they perform.

**The selected classification solution is the random forest** with 500 trees, a
depth of 5 and the `sqrt` strategy, which on the test set achieves an accuracy
of 0.9415, Cohen's kappa of 0.9284, a macro F1 measure of 0.9476 and a
multiclass AUC of 0.9966. Cross-validation did not separate the forest from the
k-nearest-neighbours method, so the choice was supplemented by consistency on
the test set, behaviour as the data volume grows, and interpretability.

**Positional roles are a continuum, not discrete categories.** This finding
appears four times independently: in the principal component plot, in the
structure of the errors of all three classifiers, in the divergence of the
silhouette coefficient and the Rand index in the clustering, and in the
composition of the resulting clusters. The unsupervised procedure recognises
three supergroups — goalkeepers, players with their centre of gravity in their
own half, and players with their centre of gravity in the opposition half — with
95.5% agreement, but not six individual positions.

**The remaining error is a property of the data, not of the methods.** All three
classifiers make errors on the same class pairs, in the same arrangement, and
none confuses classes at opposite ends of the spectrum. Progress beyond the
level achieved would more likely come from work on the features than from
further parameter tuning.

# Limitations

1. The target classes were derived from the modal position, so 25
   multi-positional players (1.5% of the dataset) have a less reliable label.
2. The models use season-level aggregates and do not take into account the
   context of an individual match or the opponent.
3. The spatial features are based on mean coordinates and dispersion, so the
   detailed structure of movement is lost.
4. No method was examined over a full combinatorial grid of hyperparameters. For
   the random forest this was even shown concretely: the combination of a large
   number of trees and a depth of 10 was not examined, and both scenarios
   suggest it as probably more favourable.
5. The cross-validation folds are not identical for all three methods — Spark
   splits at random, `caret::createFolds` stratifies.
6. The k-means method forms spherical clusters of approximately equal size. A
   density-based procedure would give complementary insight, but it has no
   distributed implementation in MLlib.
7. The clustering was performed over a set of features chosen according to their
   discriminative power with respect to position, which is a supervised
   criterion. An unsupervised analysis over a differently chosen set could
   reveal structure that has nothing to do with position.
8. A comparison with the bisecting k-means method was also attempted, which is
   interesting because bisections at the same level of the hierarchy are
   mutually independent and can be executed in parallel. The function
   `ml_bisecting_kmeans` in the version of the `sparklyr` package used returned
   a single cluster instead of the three requested, so the comparison was not
   carried out.

Possible improvements: more seasons, features by phase of play, the context of
the match score, a comparison with density-based clustering methods, and the
application of gradient boosting methods.

# Reproducibility

All scripts use a fixed seed of 42. Order of execution:

```{r reproducibility}
source("scripts/00_preuzmi_podatke.R")                 # data download
source("scripts/01_data_processing_with_sparklyr.R")   # Spark processing, features
source("scripts/03_null_values_analysis.R")            # missing values
source("scripts/04_EDA.R")                             # preliminary analysis
source("scripts/05_train_test_split.R")                # split into training and test
source("scripts/06_decision_tree.R")                   # decision tree
source("scripts/07_random_forest.R")                   # random forest
source("scripts/08_knn.R")                             # k nearest neighbours
source("scripts/09_kmeans.R")                          # clustering
```

The report is knitted with `rmarkdown::render("documentation.Rmd")`. The blocks
that start Spark are marked `eval = FALSE`; the tables are read from `results/`
and the figures from `figures/`, so knitting does not require the analysis to be
run again.

```{r session, eval=TRUE}
sessionInfo()
```

# Appendix: the complete scripts

```{r appendix, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
skripte <- c(
  "scripts/00_preuzmi_podatke.R",
  "scripts/01_data_processing_with_sparklyr.R",
  "scripts/03_null_values_analysis.R",
  "scripts/04_EDA.R",
  "scripts/05_train_test_split.R",
  "scripts/06_decision_tree.R",
  "scripts/07_random_forest.R",
  "scripts/08_knn.R",
  "scripts/09_kmeans.R"
)

for (put in skripte) {
  cat("\n\n## `", basename(put), "`\n\n", sep = "")
  if (file.exists(put)) {
    cat("```r\n"); cat(readLines(put), sep = "\n"); cat("\n```\n")
  } else {
    cat("*File not found: `", put, "`*\n", sep = "")
  }
}
```

5. MacQueen, J. (1967). *Some Methods for Classification and Analysis of Multivariate Observations*.
6. Hand, D. J. and Till, R. J. (2001). *A Simple Generalisation of the Area Under the ROC Curve for Multiple Class Classification Problems*. Machine Learning, 45, 171–186.
7. Rousseeuw, P. J. (1987). *Silhouettes: a graphical aid to the interpretation and validation of cluster analysis*. Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics, 20, 53–65.
8. Kuhn, M. *caret: Classification and Regression Training*.
9. Hechenbichler, K. and Schliep, K. *kknn: Weighted k-Nearest Neighbors*.
